notes.meaning: Paul reminds the Corinthian Christians of the good news he had brought to them earlier. They had welcomed this message and built their lives upon it. Even with all their problems, this truth remained the firm foundation where they stood.

This message of the gospel is what brings true salvation, but believers must continue holding firmly to it. If someone walks away from these central truths, their earlier profession of faith proves to be empty and useless. Real faith continues to trust what God revealed through His apostles.

Paul did not make up this message, but received it from the Lord and taught it as the most important truth. At the center of the gospel is the fact that Christ died for our sins, taking the punishment we deserved. This sacrifice fulfilled the promises written long before in the Old Testament Scriptures.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars highlight that verses 3 through 7 preserve an ancient oral creed passed down within the first two years after the crucifixion.

notes.meaning: Jesus was placed in a grave, which proved beyond doubt that His physical death was real. On the third day, God raised Him back to life, exactly as the ancient Scriptures foretold. His resurrection is a lasting victory, meaning He remains alive forever.

After He rose from the dead, Jesus appeared personally to Peter, who is also called Cephas. Next, He met with the apostles as a group, still referred to by their official title as the Twelve. These personal meetings provided solid eyewitness proof that He was truly alive.

Jesus appeared to more than five hundred followers at a single gathering, most likely in Galilee. Paul notes that most of these eyewitnesses were still living when he wrote, so readers could check their testimony directly. A few had already died, which Paul calls falling asleep because believers will awake at the resurrection.

Jesus also showed Himself to His earthly brother James, who became a respected leader in the church. After that, He met with all the apostles together before He returned to heaven. These multiple visits left no room for doubt about His return from the grave.

Last of all, the risen Lord appeared directly to Paul on the road to Damascus. Paul describes himself as one born at the wrong time, since he did not follow Jesus during His earthly ministry like the others. Seeing the living Lord gave him the full authority of an apostle while keeping him humble.

Paul viewed himself as the least among the apostles and completely unworthy of the title. Before coming to faith, he had chased down and persecuted the church of God. Remembering his past wickedness kept him modest and deeply grateful for God's mercy.

Everything good about Paul and his ministry came purely from God's free favor and grace. That grace motivated him to travel, preach, and work harder than any of the other apostles. Yet he refused to take credit for the results, confessing that God's grace within him did the work.

It made no difference whether the Corinthians heard the message from Paul or from the other apostles. All the apostles taught the exact same truth about Christ's death and resurrection. This shared gospel was the very message the Corinthians had accepted in faith.

Since the apostles clearly proclaimed that Christ rose from the dead, Paul asks why some Corinthians claimed that the dead cannot rise. These thinkers may have accepted that Jesus was alive, but rejected the idea that human bodies will be raised. Paul shows that denying the resurrection of believers contradicts the core of their faith.

If rising from the dead is completely impossible, then Christ Himself could not have been raised. Jesus had a real human body, so what applies to human bodies in general must apply to Him. Denying the resurrection of human beings destroys the truth of Christ's own victory over death.

If Jesus never rose from the grave, the message preached by the apostles is totally empty and worthless. A dead savior cannot help anyone, so faith in Him would accomplish nothing. The whole Christian faith depends completely on the reality of Jesus' resurrection.

If Christ is still dead, then the apostles are guilty of lying about God Himself. They had publicly sworn that God raised Jesus from the grave, which would be an insult to God if the dead cannot rise. It would turn God's appointed messengers into deceivers.

Paul repeats his main logic for emphasis: if dead people cannot be raised, then Christ was not raised either. The two realities cannot be pulled apart. If the grave holds all people forever, then Jesus is still buried too.

If Christ did not rise, Christian faith is pointless and people are still under the guilt and penalty of their sins. God raised Jesus to show that His sacrifice on the cross had successfully paid for human sin. Without the resurrection, there is no proof that God accepted His sacrifice, and no one is saved.

Without the resurrection, believers who have already died have completely perished. Their trust in a living Savior would have been a heartbreaking mistake. Instead of enjoying eternal peace with God, their lives would have ended in total destruction.

If trusting in Christ only helps us in this present world, Christians are more to be pitied than anyone else. Believers give up earthly pleasures and face hatred, poverty, and persecution because they look forward to eternity. Bearing all those trials for an empty promise would make them the most disappointed people on earth.

Paul leaves the gloomy suppositions behind and declares that Christ has indeed risen from the grave. In Israelite farming, the first sheaf of grain presented to God was the pledge that the full harvest would follow. In the same way, Jesus rising from death is the divine guarantee that all believers who have died will also be raised.

Physical death entered the human race through one man, Adam, when he disobeyed God. In the very same way, the resurrection of the dead comes through one man, Jesus Christ. God chose to defeat death through a real human being, reversing the harm brought by the first man.

Because all people belong to the family of Adam, every human being must face physical death. In contrast, those connected to Christ will be brought back to life through His power. Christ completely overcomes the reign of physical death that Adam started.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand 'all will be made alive' to refer only to the elect who belong to Christ, receiving bodily and spiritual life.
Many evangelicals read this to mean that every human being without exception will be raised bodily from the grave, though not all will be saved.

notes.meaning: God carries out the resurrection in a clear, orderly sequence. Christ rose first because He is the leader and source of new life for everyone else. Later, when He returns in glory, all who belong to Him will be raised to share His eternal victory.

At last the end arrives, when Christ hands over His completed kingdom to God the Father. Before this happens, He completely strips away the power of every rebellious ruler, authority, and spiritual foe. This marks the glorious finish of His assigned work to rescue and protect His people.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe Christ will reign on earth for a literal thousand years before the final end and handover described here.
Reformed Christians hold that Christ reigns from heaven throughout the church age and hands over the kingdom at His final return.

notes.meaning: Christ must continue His rule until every enemy has been completely defeated under His feet. This fulfills the prophecy in Psalm 110, where God promised that the Messiah would conquer all opposition. Believers can be sure that His reign will not stop until this victory is complete.

Death is pictured as the final enemy to be overthrown and wiped out. Other spiritual and worldly enemies are put down during Christ's reign, but death is finished when the graves are opened. Because death must be abolished, a bodily resurrection is certain.

The Old Testament states that God has placed everything under the feet of the Messiah. Paul notes the obvious exception that God the Father is not included under Christ's rule, because He is the One who granted Christ this authority. The Father remains supreme over all creation.

When all things are finally subjected to Christ, the Son will place Himself under the Father who gave Him that dominion. This does not mean the Son is inferior in His divine nature, but that His special task as Mediator has reached its goal. Then God will be clearly recognized as the supreme ruler over everything.

Paul asks what benefit comes to those who are baptized for the dead if the dead never rise at all. If the grave ends human existence, enduring baptism and identifying with those who passed away would be completely meaningless. Whatever practice the Corinthians had in mind, it showed they deep down expected the dead to live again.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars think Paul refers to a local practice of people being baptized on behalf of friends who died before baptism, which Paul mentions to make his argument without endorsing it.
